correctness.rationale: Let P=0 be any nonobtuse vertex, with incident independent edge vectors a,b and a·b≥0. The two boundary paths 0→a→a+b and 0→b→a+b each have strictly increasing radial distance: on their second edges the squared-norm derivatives are 2a·b+2t|b|² and 2a·b+2t|a|², positive for t>0; first edges increase linearly. Consequently any circle centered at P intersects each path at most once, also at shared endpoints (the union bound remains ≤2). Conversely at any polygon boundary point a sufficiently small centered circle meets either both directions of a side or both incident sides, giving ≥2. A parallelogram always has two nonobtuse angles (four in a rectangle); degenerate cases excluded. The proof is exact for all Euclidean side lengths and angles; geometric sample sweeps are corroborative only.
residual_risks: Short elementary lemma is susceptible to being rediscovered; no original new computational theorem is needed.
For a right-angle vertex the derivative vanishes only at the single endpoint t=0, not on an interval.

value.rationale: Determines a geometrically natural full class of convex bodies at the sharp constant of a historically falsified universal Erdős circle conjecture; the two-chain monotonicity provides an explicit witnessing center for all aspect ratios, including highly sheared parallelograms. This is a motivated complete classification, not an arbitrary tiny case or a parameter relabeling.
residual_risks: The argument is very short, and a referee may consider it known folklore; value is exact sharp class theorem rather than difficult technique.

final_claim: For every nondegenerate Euclidean parallelogram Q, the least possible maximum number of intersections of centered circles with its boundary equals exactly N(Q)=2; any nonobtuse vertex is a witnessing center.
limitations: Euclidean, not affine-invariant; does not extend to all centrally symmetric convex polygons.
